## Today

We go through this tutorial together. Open RStudio and type along.

1. Install `{konstats}`, the package of this course
2. Look at `{simling}`, where the data sets of the course come from
3. Practise the R basics from lecture 1, on linguistic data

## 1. konstats

### 1.1 What konstats is

`{konstats}` is the companion package of this course. It gives you:

- every package the course uses, installed with one command
- the list of lectures, with a link to each set of slides
- the exercise sheets of the tutorials
- a template for the weekly assignments

### 1.2 A folder for the course

Keep everything for the course in one folder, as an RStudio [project]{.hl}:

_File > New Project > New Directory > New Project_

. . .

Call it `statistics`, for example. When you open the project, R works inside that folder, so your files are always where R looks for them.

### 1.3 Installing konstats

`{konstats}` is not on CRAN, but on R-universe. Type this in the `Console`, once:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("konstats", repos = c("https://mcanzi.r-universe.dev",
                                       "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

. . .

This also installs every package the course uses, from the `tidyverse` and `swirl` of lecture 1 to `{simling}`. It takes a few minutes the first time.

. . .

If R asks whether to update other packages, choose `1: All`. If it asks about installing from source, answer `no`.

### 1.4 Is your computer ready?

Load the package, and check your setup:

```{r, message = TRUE}
library(konstats)
check_setup("statistics")
```

. . .

If a package is missing, the message tells you which, and what to run. Run `check_setup()` again whenever code from the course fails on your computer.

### 1.5 Lectures and slides

`lectures()` lists the lectures, with their chapters of Winter (2019) and data sets:

```{r}
lectures("statistics")[, c("number", "topic", "winter", "datasets")]
```

. . .

`slides()` opens the slides of a lecture in your browser, by number or by topic:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
slides(2)
slides("mixed models 1")
```

### 1.6 Exercise sheets

From next week, each tutorial has an exercise sheet: an R Markdown file with the exercises and an empty code chunk for each answer.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tutorials("statistics")    # which sheets there are
get_tutorial(2, ".")       # copy sheet 2 into your project folder
```

. . .

You write your answers in your copy. If the sheet is already in the folder, `get_tutorial()` stops with an error, so your answers are never overwritten.

### 1.7 Handing in homework

Tutorials 2, 4, 8, 10 and 12 end with a weekly assignment, which you hand in on Ilias.

. . .

To start the file you hand in:

_File > New File > R Markdown > From Template > Weekly assignment (konstats)_

It has a section for each exercise.

## 2. simling

### 2.1 What simling is

`{simling}` has 56 simulated data sets, from 20 branches of linguistics. From lecture 5 on, most examples in the slides use them.

. . .

The data are simulated, so we know the [true values]{.hl} behind them. You can check whether your analysis finds them.

. . .

`{konstats}` installed it already. Load it like any other package:

```{r}
library(simling)
```

### 2.2 Finding a data set

`simling_datasets()` lists all of them, with their branch, language, size, response and topic:

```{r}
simling_datasets()
```

### 2.3 A first data set

`vowel_voicing` comes from a production study: vowels before voiceless consonants (_beat_) and before voiced ones (_bead_).

```{r}
head(vowel_voicing)
```

. . .

Every data set has a help page, with what each column means and the true model behind the data:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
?vowel_voicing
```

### 2.4 A first plot

A preview of lectures 2 and 3: you do not need to understand this code yet.

```{r, fig.height = 2.9}
library(tidyverse)
ggplot(vowel_voicing, aes(x = voicing, y = duration)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = NA, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Following consonant", y = "Duration (ms)")
```

### 2.5 The true values

The help page says that the true means are 120 ms before voiceless and 160 ms before voiced consonants. The means in the data:

```{r}
tapply(vowel_voicing$duration, vowel_voicing$voicing, mean)
```

. . .

They are close to the true values, but not the same: the data are one random sample of 60 vowels per group. We come back to this in lecture 9.

## 3. R basics

### 3.1 R as a calculator

Open a new script (_File > New File > R Script_), and run each line with `Ctrl + Enter` (`Cmd + Enter` on a Mac):

```{r}
2 + 2
(3 + 2) * 4
160 - 120    # how much longer, in ms?
```

. . .

Everything after `#` is a comment. Save the script in your project folder.

### 3.2 Objects

`<-` stores a value in an object:

```{r}
voiceless <- 120
voiced <- 160
voiced - voiceless
```

. . .

Both objects now appear in the `Environment`. Names are case sensitive: `Voiced` is a different name, and no object has it.

### 3.3 Vectors

`c()` combines values into a vector. Here are five vowel durations, in ms:

```{r}
durations <- c(166, 96, 106, 112, 101)
durations / 1000    # in seconds
mean(durations)
```

. . .

What is the shortest and the longest duration? Try `min()` and `max()`.

```{r}
min(durations)
max(durations)
```

### 3.4 Indexing

Square brackets pick elements by position:

```{r}
durations[1]
durations[2:4]
durations[-1]
```

. . .

How do you get the last duration, and the first and the last together?

```{r}
durations[5]
durations[c(1, 5)]
```

### 3.5 Logical vectors

A comparison gives `TRUE` or `FALSE` for every element:

```{r}
durations > 110
durations[durations > 110]
```

. . .

How many of the five vowels are longer than 110 ms? And what proportion?

`TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0:

```{r}
sum(durations > 110)
mean(durations > 110)
```

### 3.6 Data frames

`vowel_voicing` is a data frame (a tibble): a table whose columns are vectors of the same length.

```{r}
nrow(vowel_voicing)
vowel_voicing[1:3, ]
```

. . .

`$` takes out one column, as a vector:

```{r}
mean(vowel_voicing$duration)
```

### 3.7 Your turn: one column

Using `vowel_voicing$duration`:

1. How long is the longest vowel in the data?
2. How many vowels are longer than 150 ms?
3. What proportion of vowels is longer than 150 ms?

```{r}
max(vowel_voicing$duration)
sum(vowel_voicing$duration > 150)
mean(vowel_voicing$duration > 150)
```

### 3.8 Factors

`voicing` is a factor: a column of categories, with a fixed set of levels.

```{r}
levels(vowel_voicing$voicing)
table(vowel_voicing$voicing)
```

. . .

The first level, `voiceless`, is the [reference level]{.hl}. It matters from lecture 7, when categories go into a model. In `{simling}`, the first level is always the baseline condition.

### 3.9 Functions and missing values

Functions take arguments inside their brackets:

```{r}
round(mean(vowel_voicing$duration), digits = 1)
```

. . .

`NA` is a missing value, for example a vowel whose recording failed:

```{r}
with_gap <- c(166, NA, 106)
mean(with_gap)
mean(with_gap, na.rm = TRUE)
```

### 3.10 Getting help

- `?mean` opens the help page of `mean()`, and `?vowel_voicing` works for data sets too. The examples at the bottom of a help page can be run as they are.
- An error message pasted into a search engine usually finds someone who had the same problem.

. . .

Cite the software you use:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
citation()             # R
citation("simling")    # a package
```
